missing_details: Specification that X is either a vector space of dimension n or a matroid of rank n
Definition of a basis in the context of vector spaces or matroids
Requirement that there are exactly n bases B₁,…,Bₙ which are pairwise disjoint as subsets of the ground set
Construction of an n×n array (matrix) whose rows are the given bases B_i
Condition that each column of the matrix must itself be a basis of X
Equivalent notion of a 'transversal' or 'rainbow' basis selecting exactly one element from each B_i
refined_question: Let X be either a vector space of dimension n over a field or a matroid of rank n, and let B₁, B₂, …, Bₙ be n pairwise disjoint bases of X. Does there always exist an n×n array [x_{i,j}] of elements of X such that for each row index i, the set {x_{i,1},…,x_{i,n}} equals B_i, and for each column index j, the set {x_{1,j},…,x_{n,j}} is also a basis of X?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, given n disjoint bases B₁,…,Bₙ of X, can one always find n disjoint ‘transversal’ bases C₁,…,Cₙ, each consisting of exactly one element from each B_i?
justification: The original conjecture name refers only to bases but does not specify the domain (vector spaces vs. matroids), the number and disjointness of bases, the matrix construction, or the requirement on columns; thus the name alone scores low on completeness. We have added all necessary definitions (X, bases, disjointness, matrix arrangement, column-basis condition) to make the statement standalone and faithful to the canonical formulation in the lead section of the Wikipedia article.
